hook: "Picking the right ad format used to be a bet you only got to place once."
idea: AI generation killed the one-format bet — the street quiz is one of the batch formats: 'Are you an average American? $50, five questions, get three right' — ship quiz + review + GRWM + DITL together and let the feed vote.
sequencing: Past constraint: one format, one expensive bet.
The unlock: generate all formats at once.
The example: $50 street quiz video + transcript.
The method: run batch, feed picks winner.
Payoff: format in a weekend, price of lunch.
CTA: article.
formatting: Thesis post + 27s street-quiz video with full transcript ('Are you an average American? … $50. Five questions…').
why_it_works: The transcript shows the quiz mechanics: stakes ($50), simple rules (3 of 5), escalating questions, lifeline ('phone a friend') — participation hooks that hold to the last frame.
what_to_steal: The street-quiz transcript as LC's quiz template: 'Are you a jewelry expert? $50, five questions' — filmed (or AI-generated) street quizzes where the prize is LC credit. The quiz format belongs in every LC format batch.

hook: "You do not need to know how to edit. Here are 12 video formats that have built $10,000 months for people who cannot cut a video"
cta: Telegram link in bio — free production template.
idea: Quiz formats (#3: guess the country/logo/age) hold viewers to the last frame because they want to be right — ranked in the fastest-to-monetize tier alongside would-you-rather and rankings.
sequencing: Hook: no editing needed, $10K months.
Fastest tier: text story, would-you-rather, guess-the-X quizzes, rankings, fact lists.
The quiz insight: holds to last frame — viewers want to be right.
Mid tier: restoration, industrial, lyrics, recipes, timelines.
Highest tier: money explainers, gear breakdowns.
The 60-second picker: match goal to tier.
The template rule: free app, one voice, captions, screen change every 2-3s.
CTA: telegram template.
formatting: Tiered how-to: 12 formats grouped FASTEST/MID/HIGHEST pay, each one line + the 'pick in 60 seconds' decision tree.
why_it_works: 'They want to be right' names the exact retention mechanism of quizzes — self-testing. The tiered picker turns a list into a decision tool.
what_to_steal: The quiz-retention insight for LC: 'guess the price' / 'real vs fake' jewelry quizzes hold viewers to the last frame — LC's 'guess which one is waterproof' quiz is a retention machine. The production rule (captions on every word, screen change every 2-3s) is LC's editing spec.

hook: "10 content formats that ACTUALLY work (proven by our own creators):"
idea: Ten agency-proven organic formats — ranking and tier list among them — the quiz/guess-adjacent formats that drive participation.
sequencing: Hook: 10 formats that ACTUALLY work.
The list: storytelling through before/after.
The proof claim: proven by our own creators — agency-cred framing.
Implicit close: the list is the deliverable.
formatting: 10-item proven-format list, one per line. Terse agency-cred format.
why_it_works: 'ACTUALLY work (proven by our own creators)' is anti-guru positioning — proof over theory.
what_to_steal: Ranking/tier-list as LC's quiz-adjacent organic formats: 'ranking my jewelry collection' / 'jewelry tier list' — participation + debate in one.

hook: "My Facebook Ad Creative Styles Tier List (2026)"
idea: 2026 paid-format tiers: reaction lands S-tier — the closest quiz/guess relative — while the list omits pure quiz formats, suggesting they're organic-first.
sequencing: Hook: tier list.
S-tier incl. reaction.
A-tier list.
C-tier: unboxing, DITL.
Link.
why_it_works: Tier lists drive debate; the S-tier reaction slot is the actionable prior.
what_to_steal: Reaction at S-tier validates LC's reaction-style quiz content ('watch her guess the price') for paid; pure quizzes stay organic.
